eyebrow: Python for Data Science · Chapter 4, Lesson 18
subtitle: SQL's JOIN and UNION ALL — merge and concat in pandas.

code:
m = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id")

# default is an INNER join —
# customer 106 (no orders) vanishes
caption: The output is ordered by customer, not by order — don't assume merge preserves row order.

code:
left = customers.merge(orders, on="customer_id", how="left")
# all 6 customers; Fay Park gets NaN order columns

# how: "inner", "left", "right", "outer"
caption: A whole-number column (order_id) becomes a decimal once it receives a missing value, in pandas 1.x.

code:
c2 = customers.merge(orders, on="customer_id",
                      how="left", indicator=True)
c2[c2["_merge"] == "left_only"][["customer_id", "name"]]
caption: The pandas version of a LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL anti-join — great for auditing a merge.

code:
o2 = orders.rename(columns={"customer_id": "cust_id"})
o2.merge(customers, left_on="cust_id", right_on="customer_id")

# same-name non-key columns get _x / _y, or use suffixes=(...)
caption: left_on/right_on handle mismatched key names — suffixes names the overlap clash instead of _x/_y.
A duplicated key on the lookup side repeats matching rows and inflates totals — validate catches it loudly.
join is a shortcut for merging on the index, defaulting to a left join — most people just use merge for everything.

code:
jan = orders[orders["order_date"] < "2024-02-01"]
rest = orders[orders["order_date"] >= "2024-02-01"]
pd.concat([jan, rest], ignore_index=True)
caption: Like UNION ALL — ignore_index=True renumbers from 0 instead of keeping duplicate original labels.

eyebrow: A very common pattern: merge a summary back
code:
tot = (orders.groupby("customer_id", as_index=False)["amount"].sum()
       .rename(columns={"amount": "total"}))
customers.merge(tot, on="customer_id", how="left")
# Fay Park -> NaN total (no orders)
caption: Aggregate first, then merge the aggregate onto another table — whether NaN becomes 0 is your call.
